newsitem.title: ITALY: Thousands of Italians protest at austerity budget.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Italians protest at austerity budget.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of Italians marched through Rome on Saturday to protest at the government's 1997 austerity budget, as former premier Silvio Berlusconi and his allies said Italian democracy was at risk.

Centre-left Prime Minister Romano Prodi's austerity budget aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from the deficit next year to meet the level needed for membership in Europe's economic and monetary union.
The package contains fresh taxes including a one-off "Euro Tax" designed to bring in some 12 trillion ($7.8 million) to help Italy be part of monetary union scheduled for 1999.
"We ask that this "Euro Tax', which will be never get us into Europe anyway, be abolished," Berlusconi said.

The centre-right opposition kicked off the mass protest in two spots, at the southern Via Tuscolana and near the Vatican in the northwest, before converging on the central Piazza San Giovanni in Laterno.

Berlusconi and other leaders were due to join the march for a few kilometres (miles) before addressing the crowd in the piazza, a tradtional bastion for left-wing protests, but waited until marchers passed their hotel before venturing out.

"There were so many people marching through the streets in support of this cause that we had to wait in here," Berlusconi told state television's RAI3. Organisers said up to 300,000 were taking part in the march.
When the centre-right leaders reached the piazza, they raised their fists in triumph to the cheering crowd.
One protester, dressed as Prodi with a long Pinocchio nose, told televison: "Being Prodi, I can promise all Italians that I will absolutely not raise taxes."
Another demonstrator had a strange silver gadget latched on his back. "This machine measures how much air you breath so the government can tax you accordingly," he said.

The hardleft Communist Refoundation party was simultaneously holding a demonstration in the southern port city of Naples to protest at unemployment. The party said up to 150,000 people took part in the protest.
But the Rome march took centre stage as a visibly enraged Berlusconi lashed out at RAI3, accusing the state channel of trying to discredit the protest in its live coverage.
"Shame!" the media magnate screamed, his face turning red.
"In all my years in television, never have I seen anything so improper," he added. "It is an insult to the demonstrators and all Italian moderates. We are already in a regime. Shame!"
Prodi said he was suprised to see Berlusconi so furious.

"I was struck to see Berlusconi so angry, but I am serene and realise the entire country is not out in the piazzas, and I am convinced that the majority can carry out its work," Prodi told television.

Rocco Buttiglione, leader of a small Roman Catholic party allied with Berlusconi, slammed the government for trying to use proxy powers to dictate policy on sensitive budget areas like tax, without requiring subsequent parliamentary approval.
"They are trying to pass a budget without parliament's help. This is a dictatorship," Buttiglione said.
The budget is now under exam in parliament's lower house. Once the Chamber of Deputies ratifies it, the bill moves to the Senate with final approval by the end of year.
